body:
Assimp checks the file extension first. `.STP` is not listed as supported by the IFC importer, and neither by any other importer, so that fails.

After that, Assimp looks at the beginning of the file and searches for keywords. IFC will pick up `ISO-10303-21`, and that would be fine. But the DXF importer runs its analysis *before* IFC, and it matches the keyword `HEADER`, which is contained in every STEP file. So Assimp decides it’s a DXF file.

There are two ways to correct this:
1. Extend the IFC loader to support the file extension `.STP`, so it always matches on the first try.
2. Change the DXF loader to not look for `HEADER` alone, but only if following `SECTION` a few lines above. Or matching `HEADER` followed by a line break, but never `HEADER;` followed by a semicolon.

From [the DXF specification](https://images.autodesk.com/adsk/files/autocad_2012_pdf_dxf-reference_enu.pdf), page 217, I understand that you identify a DXF by matching: `whitespace "0" whitespace "SECTION" whitespace "2" whitespace "HEADER" whitespace`

Does Assimp already include the necessary facilities for that (e.g. regex search)?

**Notice:** Don’t get your STEP hopes too high. It’s a very complicated format and I have only ever seen Assimp load two IFC files, but fail on hundreds of others.

> Assimp checks the file extension first. `.STP` is not listed as supported by the IFC importer, and neither by any other importer, so that fails.

It *is* listed as supported by the IFC importer, though. 

The following code:

```
        Assimp::Importer importer;
        unsigned index;
        cout << importer.IsExtensionSupported("stp") << endl;
        cout << (index = importer.GetImporterIndex("stp")) << endl;
        cout << importer.GetImporterInfo(index)->mFileExtensions << endl;
        set<string> extns;
        importer.GetImporter(index)->GetExtensionList(extns);
        for (string e : extns)
            cout << e << endl;
        cout << (importer.GetImporter(index) == importer.GetImporter("stp")) << endl;
```

Outputs:

```
1
39
ifc ifczip stp
ifc
ifczip
stp
1
```

Also it's reflected in the output of the other test program, up at the start (I glossed over it in my post):

```
assimp 5.0.1 (master @ cd42b995)
Extension: "stp"
  IsExtensionSupported:       true
  GetImporterIndex:           39
  GetImporter:                plugin=0x0000015974491640
  ->GetExtensionList:         ifc ifczip stp
  ->GetInfo->mName:           Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) Importer
  ->GetInfo->mFileExtensions: ifc ifczip stp
```

> Change the DXF loader...

Note that the STL loader picked up one of the files, too. And so did the X3D importer (although that seems to be a consequence of *no* importers trying to load it, see linked issue).

@krishty I just did a bunch more testing; the details are boring but long story short I *can* at least confirm that you're onto something regarding the order of the tested importers.

> There are two ways to correct this:

Based on my observations, let me propose two additional, more generic ways to correct this:

1. When enumerating importers and testing `CanRead`, try the one reported as supporting the file's extension (if it has one) *first*, no matter what.
2. A less trivial option could be to have `CanRead` return some sort of *well-defined* confidence level -- e.g. NO, MAYBE, YES -- and choose the importer with the most confident non-NO result (choosing the first if multiple are found with the same result).

Although, as you say, the DXF importer's heuristics should probably also be improved (and apparently the STL loader as well). That should happen *regardless* of STEP file issues.

**Fun fact:** You propose to add ` || extension == "stp"`. If you look at IFCLoader.cpp (117), you’ll see that it should pick up the `.stp` extension, but in line 131 that it shouldn’t. Line 117 has no effect, but I’d argue that it should.

I had a brief look at the format detection and tl;dr it is a train wreck. There seem to be three different mechanisms at work, and every importer uses them differently. To the point where importers [define functions which cannot ever be used](https://github.com/assimp/assimp/pull/3796) because there is so much confusion around the way of declaring an importer to match a certain format.

I’m now trying to clean this up globally, but lots of things are going to break …

> When enumerating importers and testing CanRead, try the one reported as supporting the file's extension (if it has one) first, no matter what.

Yeah, but there’s the little problem that multiple importers can use the same extension – e.g. XML could be both Irrlicht or COLLADA. So I tried searching for extensions, and after that, doing deep detection. But this breaks FBX because FBX detection just works for ASCII FBX and rejects binary FBX(!). This is going to cost some nerves …

P.S.: Sorry, I didn’t see your other comment!

> It _is_ listed as supported by the IFC importer, though.

Haha, yes! That’s because that list is generated by a different mechanism (`aiImporterDesc::mFileExtensions`, the one in IFC line 117). One mechanism is only for GUI (`aiImporterDesc::mFileExtensions`, which is evaluated by `GetExtensionList()`), another mechanism does the actual work (`BaseImporter::CanRead()`). They are entirely different and at the same time redundant. It’s insanity.

I’ll remove any file extension checks from `CanRead()` and handle them exclusively via `aiImporterDesc::mFileExtensions` and `GetExtensionList()`, so that it all syncs up.

> Yeah, but there’s the little problem that multiple importers can use the same extension – e.g. XML could be both Irrlicht or COLLADA. So I tried searching for extensions, and after that, doing deep detection. But this breaks FBX because FBX detection just works for ASCII FBX and rejects binary FBX(!). This is going to cost some nerves …

Well, the approach I was thinking there (which may make no sense, I don't have a good grasp of assimp's internals) would be to not only prioritize the loader that is associated with the extension, but to *also* improve the heuristics in various `CanRead`s, so that `CanRead` would still make an ultimate decision but it would just so happen that the prioritized importer would be checked *first*. So in your example, e.g.:

- Make the Irrlicht `CanRead` check for the appropriate XML node.
- Make the COLLADA `CanRead` check for the appropriate XML node.
- When searching for importers, just search for ones that say they handle ".xml" first, then search the rest. 

Essentially that proposal was to do a stable sort on the importer list where the only criteria for `<` is basically (pseudo code):

```
    extension = ...;
    stable_sort(importers, [extension] (importer1, importer2) {
        return importer1.registeredFor(extension) && !importer2.registeredFor(extension);
    });
```

Also, I see that `checkSig` parameter, what if the ordering went something like this:

- Prioritize importers by extension as proposed above. Let's also define *matching* as the list of importers that are registered for that extension, and *nonmatching* as the rest of the importers (stable sort so both lists maintain relative order of global list). 
- Now, search importers in this order, stopping as soon as an appropriate importer is found:
   1. If *size(matching) > 1* then search through *matching* with *checkSig = true*.
   2. Search through *matching* with *checkSig = false*.
   3. Search through *nonmatching* with *checkSig = false*.
   4. If *size(matching) == 1* then search through *matching* with *checkSig = true* (otherwise we already did this in 1).
   5. Search through *nonmatching* with *checkSig = true*.

In other words:
- If only one importer is registered for this extension just use it (probably; i.e. *checkSig = false*).
- If more than one is registered, though, do a content-based check to disambiguate.
- If we somehow still haven't figured it out, just search all the other importers, falling back on content-based as a last resort.
- Try our best to minimize / defer content-based searches for performance, really.

Now, in that ordering, it's pretty improbable that you'd ever get to step 3, really, at least with the current implementations of `CanRead`, since they just do extension matching when *checkSig == false* and we already know they match the extensions. But, whatever, I picked that ordering to allow for lots of flexibility in `CanRead` implementations.

In any case, I don't think there's any way to completely avoid globally improving `GetRead`s, but with some analysis and careful planning you might be able to minimize it. I'd be happy to help, especially with code review and planning, if you need another carbon-based neural network to process it.

(Oh, as an aside, I also separately confirmed that the IFC loader can't actually load any of my test models, lol -- I tested by forcing the use of that loader. I'm about to report that as a separate issue, so I don't want to get into details here.)

issue.body:
The search for a matching importer had a few issues, see #3791. There were two different mechanisms to determine whether an importer accepts a specific file extension:
1. `aiImporterDesc::mFileExtensions`, which was forwarded to the UI via `BaseImporter::GetExtensionList()`.
2. `BaseImporter::CanRead()` when called with `checkSig == false`, which determines whether to actually use that importer.

They were redundant and got out of sync repeatedly. I removed 2. completely and replaced it with 1., thereby syncing UI/import and shortening all `BaseImporter::CanRead()` implementations.

Further bugfixes:
- fixed glTF2 importer throwing exceptions when checking whether it can load a file
- removed `BaseImporter::SimpleExtensionCheck()` because it is no longer used and had a bug with case sensitivity

Since the `checkSig` parameter in `BaseImporter::CanRead()` is now useless, it can be removed completely. I’m not sure if this would break ABI compatiblity, so I’ll submit it with a later pull request.

That’s pretty much what I’ve done now. I have eliminated `checkSig == false` completely because it was redundant with the file extension registry.

I'd be happy to help, especially with code review and planning, if you need another carbon-based neural network to process it.

Thanks a lot! Please look at my pull request above and test that version for yourself. CI won’t run on my pull requests until @kimkulling closes my older ones, but from running `unit.exe` on my machine it seems like I didn’t break any tests. STP properly triggers the IFC loader now, case sensitive extensions work better than before, we lost 400 lines of useless code and 9 KiB in the executable. Looks good, but with such large changes we need to be sure.

Yes, `CanRead()` needs drastic improvement. I can improve the STL loader’s via [one of my own projects](https://papas-best.com/stlviewer_en), and I’ll look at my own FBX detection code. But I probably don’t have the time to do much more than that.

issue.body:
In doing some testing (assimp 5.0.1 64-bit, release build, dynamic linkage, Windows 10 64-bit, MSVC 2019) I've discovered a number of issues particularly centered around exporting models then re-importing them. I'm going to list what I've noticed here. Some of these may be bugs, some may not, some may be user error, some may be known about or fixed in the latest revision.

I apologize for cramming everything into one report, but I just wanted to mention them all in case there is something new here.

Here's the things I noticed:

- `aiGetVersionRevision()` returns 0 instead of 1 for assimp 5.0.1 (so the version is reported as 5.0.0).
- Nothing that the Step exporter wrote was able to be read by the StepFile importer. However, with validation turned off, the importer actually reported success, but the scene was empty. Also the scene flags were 0 despite it being incomplete. With validation on, it failed ("Validation failed: A node of the scenegraph is NULL"). 
- Nothing that the GL Transmission Format 1.0 ASCII exporter wrote (id="gltf") was able to be read by the GLTF importer. All produced the error "class DeadlyImportError: GLTF: Unsupported glTF version: 1.0". Additionally, unlike the other importers, even on failure here the importer did not set its "importerIndex" property. Note that glb, glb2, and gltf2 all seemed OK. Only gltf failed on re-import.
- The x3d importer set the AI_SCENE_FLAGS_ALLOW_SHARED flag in every scene. I don't think this is a problem, just pointing it out because none of the other importers tested set that. 
- Surprisingly, neither assxml nor assjson have a corresponding importer? This seems strange, since they're library-defined formats. Did I miss something? Both lead to "No suitable reader found for the file format of file..." errors on import.
- Nothing that the 3MF exporter wrote was able to be read by the 3MF importer. As with the step files, the importer still reported success with validation turned off and did not set any scene flags, despite the scene containing 0 meshes. With validation on, import failed with "Validation failed: aiScene::mNumMeshes is 0. At least one mesh must be there". Additionally, nothing that the 3MF exporter wrote was able to be read by Windows Paint 3D, which supports the format.
- The Blender 3D Importer has a newline in its name. It is the only importer with a newline. It can be problematic in GUIs.

That's the summary. Some notes / suggestions I have on that:

- The functions in version.h should probably return the correct version.
- The Step file importer should fail or at least set AI_SCENE_FLAGS_INCOMPLETE if it can't load any meshes (although really, it should be able to import files that the exporter writes).
- Same for the 3MF importer: It also should fail or at least set the appropriate scene flags if it can't load any meshes.
- The files written by the 3MF exporter couldn't be read in Windows 10's Paint 3D software either. I didn't try any other software, though.
- Even though the "importerIndex" property appears undocumented, and this is a bit of an edge case, for consistency the GLTF importer should probably set it even on failure, since the importer *is* known (GLTF). 
- "Unsupported GLTF Version: 1.0" is an odd error to get for the GLTF 1.0 importer. :) Only seems to affect ASCII format.
- There should be an importer for assxml and assjson, no?
- The newline before the URL in the Blender importer's name should be removed. It might also make sense to move the URL to the comments field instead, like many of the other importers.

---

The test application I wrote (not designed for general consumption, so please file complaints into the 🗑️, lol) can be found [here](https://github.com/JC3/ModelSplit/tree/master/generate_test_models) (it does not actually depend on Qt and should be compilable without it, there's just one source file). The program performs the following operations for every exporter:

- Export a scene with 1 mesh, then re-import it with no pp flags.
- Export a scene with 5 meshes, then re-import it with no pp flags.
- Export a scene with 1 mesh, then re-import it with data validation.
- Export a scene with 5 meshes, then re-import it with data validation.

Each scene has one or more meshes (each mesh is a basic tetrahedron) that have vertex coords, faces, and nothing else. The scene has 1 material, and 1 node. That node also has all of the meshes. It's possible that some of these failed because some required info was missing, in which case, pay no mind to those. 🤷‍♂️

It then generates a report of the import results (importer used, scene flags on import, errors, etc.), as well as a report listing *all* importers associated with a compatible exporter (which is what I was originally testing before I got sidetracked by this).

The report it generates can be found on [Google Sheets](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1sTFfHnc7aDZLzDbOZ7TuHCmA29oIWnLbtvBmGq-FmhY/edit?usp=sharing). I'm not going to describe it because I just summarized it above.

I hope this was useful. If I can, I'll do my best to submit some actual patches (also like I said I haven't checked out the latest master yet I'm on the 5.0.1 release, so it's possible a lot of this is moot), but I'm not sure if I'll have a chance to any time soon.
